title: Breguet Classique Phase de Lune in 18 k Rose gold ref 7137
description: Founded in Paris in 1775 by Swiss-born horologist Abraham-Louis Breguet, the House of Breguet is one of the oldest and most influential names in watchmaking. Often referred to as the "Leonardo da Vinci of watchmaking," Breguet transformed the art of horology with groundbreaking inventions, including the tourbillon and the self-winding movement. The design of this Breguet Classique 7137 can be traced back to the legendary Perpetuelle No. 5 , a quarter-repeating pocket watch completed by Abraham-Louis Breguet in 1794. Its modern interpretation began in 1983 with the introduction of the reference 3137, designed by the celebrated watchmaker Daniel Roth. Over the following decades, the model evolved into today's reference 7137 while faithfully preserving the timeless aesthetics and technical spirit of Breguet's original creation. The tasteful 39 mm case is crafted from 18k rose gold and features Breguet's signature fluted caseband, soldered straight lugs, and a sapphire display case back offering a view of the beautifully finished Calibre 502.3 DR1 automatic movement, complete with an off-centred solid gold oscillating weight. The silvered gold dial is a showcase of traditional engine-turning craftsmanship. The power reserve indicator is decorated with a panier maillé (basket-weave) guilloché, the date subdial features a damier (checkerboard) pattern, while the main dial is finished in the iconic clous de Paris (hobnail) motif. with a monnphase indicator .As is customary with Breguet, the individual serial number is proudly engraved on the dial, complemented by the brand's instantly recognizable blued open-tipped Breguet hands. The watch is paired with the shown slightly used original Breguet leather strap , fitted with a 18 k original 18k pink gold Breguet folding clasp. The watch has been fully serviced by our watchmaker ensuring years of enjoyment . We believe the Classique collection remains one of the most undervalued segments of haute horlogerie, offering an extraordinary level of craftsmanship and history for the price! title: Rolex Cosmograph Daytona 6263 Big Red Floating Silver Soleil Dial
description: The Rolex Daytona 6263 stands in a league of its own. Introduced alongside its sister reference, the 6265, it represents the final and most developed chapter of Rolex’s manual-wind chronograph era. With its screw-down pushers, Oyster case construction and black bakelite bezel, the 6263 brought both a stronger sportier look and improved water resistance over the earlier pump-pusher models — key traits that helped define the legendary Daytona formula collectors remain so drawn to today. Produced over a long period, the reference saw a number of dial variations, with certain executions becoming true collector favourites. Among them, the silver soleil “Big Red” is without question one of the most celebrated. The nickname refers to the large red “DAYTONA” signature curved above the 6 o’clock register — a small detail perhaps, but one that completely changes the personality of the watch. On the best examples, like this one, it gives the dial that extra spark collectors instantly fall for. This particular watch is especially compelling thanks to its outstanding overall condition. The case is incredibly strong, with sharp and even lugs that give it the crisp, well-preserved profile collectors are always hoping to find. The silver soleil dial, itself being slightly rarer due to it’s floating Big Red designation, is beautifully clean and completely mark-free, with all lume plots still intact and aged to a warm vanilla tone. The chronograph registers are equally clean and have taken on a subtle brown discolouration that adds depth, warmth and a wonderful sense of character. It is exactly this kind of honest and attractive ageing that gives a great vintage Daytona its soul. The Mk4 bakelite bezel is in excellent condition, free from cracks or blemishes, and the watch retains its correct period Mk1 pushers. Inside beats the legendary Valjoux 727-based movement, freshly serviced by our watchmaker, and the watch is fitted with a Rolex 78350 Oyster bracelet with 557B endlinks and M4 clasp code. There is a reason the Daytona has inspired generations of collectors and remains one of the most admired chronographs in the vintage world. The great ones have a presence that goes far beyond specifications alone. This 6263 has exactly that feeling — iconic, beautifully preserved and full of charisma. A truly attractive “Big Red” Daytona with all the right details and that unmistakable grail-like appeal. title: Patek Philippe Perpetual Calendar 3940J Early Second Series in 18k yellow gold with Box and Extract of the Archives
description: While watch trends may come and go, the perpetual calendar remains a timeless favourite among seasoned collectors. We are therefore delighted to offer one of the rarest variations of this modern classic—and a grail for many—the Patek Philippe reference 3940. The aesthetically balanced 3940 was originally introduced in 1985 in a limited run of just 25 pieces to celebrate the 225th anniversary of Beyer Chronometrie. Following this special edition, the reference was released to the wider public and went on to enjoy an impressive production run. Collectors often favour the earlier series, and this example is no exception. The early 3940 dials have a distinctive, more vintage-inspired layout that sets them apart from the later versions. This particular example, crafted in 18k yellow gold, features the highly collectible “early” second-series dial, which, in our opinion, is one of the most beautiful variations of the 3940. The “earlier” second-series dial is significantly rarer than the later versions and can be identified by several subtle yet important details. The day and month sub-dials feature distinctive double-step bevelled edges, giving them greater depth and visual presence, while the subsidiary seconds dial at 3 o’clock is notably free of the crosshair found on the later iterations. This transitional dial variant was produced for only a short period between 1987 and 1989 and in much more limited numbers, with approximately 800 examples believed to have been made. Its rarity, combined with these unique dial characteristics, makes it a particularly interesting configuration for collectors. The dial itself is a masterclass in balance and subtle sophistication, with plenty of character hidden in its smallest details. But the real star is beneath it: Patek Philippe’s calibre 240Q perpetual calendar movement. Introduced during the height of the quartz crisis—a period that threatened the future of traditional Swiss watchmaking—the 3940 was a bold statement from Patek Philippe. Its ultra-thin calibre 240Q allowed the brand to house a full perpetual calendar in a beautifully proportioned 36mm case, creating what would become one of the maison’s defining modern complications. The case remains beautifully balanced and is fitted with the correct solid case-back. The watch is accompanied by an official Extract from the Archives and Patek Philippe service papers from 2020. The calendar displays are in French—a charming and romantic detail and, for collectors, one of the absolute rarest configurations. Fitted with a supple Bulang and son's leather strap and its original Patek Philippe gold pin buckle, this 3940 ticks every box for the discerning collector. The watch has also been fully checked by our watchmaker. We have a real soft spot for the 3940. It remains one of the most underappreciated references in Patek Philippe’s storied catalogue, despite offering almost everything a serious collector could want: an iconic ultra-thin movement, perpetual calendar

title: Rolex Oyster Perpetual 1500 Silver Underline Dial in 14k Yellow Gold
description: The Rolex Oyster Perpetual Date in 34mm debuted in the mid-1950s, following the introduction of the 36mm Datejust in 1945. It offered a slightly smaller alternative, combining the waterproof Oyster case, self-winding Perpetual movement and the signature Cyclops magnifying lens over the date window. The specimen at hand is crafted in 14k yellow gold, an unusual feature for Rolex. During the 1940s through the mid-1980s, Rolex produced 14k gold watches primarily for the North American market, where high import duties were imposed on 18k gold watches. By using 14k gold cases—often manufactured in the United States by case makers such as Star Watch Case Co. or D&A to Rolex specifications—the brand could significantly reduce the final retail cost for American customers. The case and smooth bezel are in wonderfully preserved condition and are complemented by a lovely silver dial with an especially interesting detail: a small “Underline” positioned just above the 6 o’clock marker. The term “Underline” refers to this small horizontal line printed on the dial, a feature found on various Rolex models during the early 1960s. Its exact production period varies according to the model, reference and dial configuration. Rolex never officially documented the meaning of the underline, which is part of what makes these dials so fascinating to collectors. The most widely accepted theory is that it relates to the transition in luminous materials during this period, as Rolex moved away from radium-based luminous compounds towards tritium. The underline should therefore not simply be interpreted as a universal “tritium” marking. Rolex used several different dial designations during this transitional period, and the precise meaning remains dependent on the specific reference, production period and dial configuration. What is certain is that underline dials were produced for a relatively limited period, making surviving examples particularly appealing to vintage Rolex collectors. Further adding to the character of this dial is its “Swiss” only designation, elegant applied hour markers and beautifully sharp dauphine hands.The watch comes on one of our Bulang and sons leather straps and is fitted with a plaque Rolex pin buckle. A charming and unusual Rolex Oyster Perpetual Date, combining the warmth of 14k yellow gold with a beautifully preserved early-1960s dial and one of those subtle period details that makes vintage Rolex collecting so rewarding ! title: Omega Speedmaster 145.022-69 Grey Racing dial with Original Box and Booklet
description: The Omega Speedmaster is one of the world's most iconic chronographs, originally launched in 1957 as a racing and sports watch. It was the first chronograph to feature a tachymeter scale on the external bezel rather than the dial, improving readability for racing drivers. In the early 1960s, NASA secretly acquired chronographs from several manufacturers to determine which would be suitable for its astronauts. After surviving a series of brutal qualification tests—including extreme temperatures, violent shocks, vibrations, acceleration, and decompression—the Speedmaster was the only watch to pass. In 1965, NASA officially certified it for all manned space missions . Its most legendary moment came on July 21, 1969 (UTC), when astronaut Buzz Aldrin stepped onto the lunar surface during the Apollo 11 mission while wearing his Speedmaster. This historic achievement forever cemented the watch's place in history and earned it its enduring nickname: the "Moonwatch." If you are looking for a truly rare and historically significant Omega Speedmaster, look no further. Produced in a limited run of approximately 150 pieces, this reference is widely regarded as Omega's first limited-production Speedmaster, making it one of the most collectible vintage Speedmasters ever produced. Although the Speedmaster Mark II is best known for its colourful "Racing Dial," it remains something of a mystery why Omega produced a small batch of these dials for the reference 145.022. Whether it was a market test, an experiment to gauge demand, or an attempt to appeal to motorsport enthusiasts, no official explanation has ever surfaced. Whatever the reason, it is estimated that only around 150 examples were cased, making this one of the rarest and most desirable Speedmasters in existence. The classic asymmetrical 42 mm stainless steel case is in wonderful condition. The case back retains a well-defined hippocampus medallion, and we have deliberately chosen to leave the watch untouched, as we found no evidence that it has ever been polished. The original tachymeter bezel remains in very nice condition and features the coveted "Dot Over Ninety" (DON) configuration, while the original Omega-signed hesalite crystal is still fitted. The distinctive grey "Racing Dial" immediately catches the eye with its vivid orange accents, matching orange hands, and soft red outer minute track. These vibrant colours give the watch tremendous wrist presence—we've even included a photograph taken under UV light, where the dial truly comes alive. The watch is fitted with the correct Omega reference 1039 flat-link bracelet with 516 end links and a clasp stamped 2/70. Inside beats the legendary hand-wound calibre 861, fully checked and regulated and bearing a movement number within the correct range documented for the other known Racing Dial Speedmasters. Whether these watches were intended as a limited-production experiment or simply a bold exploration of a more colourful Speedmaster, we may never know.

The caseback carries the distinctive “D-H” engraving, standing for “Deutsches Heer” (German Army), together with the military issue numbers. The gilt dial is in nice condition as well, with small seconds at 6 o’clock and large Arabic numerals filled with lume. Inside is Longines’ beautifully finished calibre 12.68Z, a classic hand-wound movement with Geneva stripes and plenty of old-school Longines charm. And to make the package even more interesting, this watch comes accompanied by an Extract from the Longines Archives, confirming delivery to Germany in 1943. The watch has also been fully serviced by our watchmaker. A rare bit of WWII watch history, and certainly not your everyday Longines. This is the kind of watch that makes us stop, look twice and dig a little deeper. Get in touch! Fast forward to 1978, and Cartier gave the Santos a more contemporary feel with the introduction of the Santos Carrée. Its exposed screws, integrated bracelet and steel-and-gold construction gave the classic design a sportier edge. Then, in 1987, Cartier softened things up with the Santos Galbée. The name refers to the curved case, with its rounded contours and bracelet designed to sit more comfortably around the wrist. The ref. 2319 belongs to this later Galbée generation, particularly associated with the 1990s and early 2000s. A great-looking Santos Galbée with plenty of classic Cartier character—and exactly the kind of watch that looks even better once it’s on the wrist! title: Omega Cal.28.9 Two-Tone Dial Screw Down Case Chronograph
description: The history of Omega began in 1848, when 23-year-old watchmaker Louis Brandt established a small watchmaking workshop in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland. Over the following 175 years, the company evolved from a modest atelier into one of the world’s most celebrated luxury watch manufacturers, renowned for its achievements in precision timekeeping, space exploration, professional diving watches, and mechanical innovation. The Omega Calibre 28.9 (often designated as Cal. 28.9 CHRO) is historically significant as Omega’s first compact wrist chronograph movement, produced in very limited numbers between 1932 and approximately 1943. Developed in partnership with Lemania — where it was known as the Lemania 13CH — this 28.9 mm movement laid the foundation for Omega’s iconic sports and military chronographs, eventually evolving into the legendary Calibre 321 used in the first NASA-approved Speedmaster. It is closely related to the Calibre 33.3, but considerably rarer, especially in a case configuration such as this example. title: Patek Philippe Calatrava in 18k Yellow Gold Silver Soleil Dial ref. 3470 Ultra-Thin
description: The Patek Philippe Calatrava is widely regarded as the quintessential dress watch. Introduced in 1932, it was created during one of the most challenging periods in the manufacture's history, shortly after the Stern family acquired Patek Philippe amid the Great Depression. The Calatrava embodied a new design philosophy—one of timeless elegance and understated sophistication—that would come to define the brand. Its minimalist aesthetic was heavily inspired by the German Bauhaus movement, embracing the principle that "form follows function." Every element was reduced to its purest expression, resulting in a watch whose restrained design remains as relevant today as it was nearly a century ago. The model takes its name from the Calatrava Cross, the medieval emblem adopted by Patek Philippe as its official trademark in 1887. More than ninety years after its introduction, the Calatrava remains one of the most influential dress watches ever created and continues to serve as the benchmark for elegant watch design. Offered here is a mid-1960s Patek Philippe Calatrava reference 3470 in 18k yellow gold. Its elegant 30 mm case features straight lugs, a small winding crown, and a snap-on case back, creating the perfectly balanced proportions that define vintage Calatravas. The silver soleil dial is beautifully understated, featuring painted black Roman numerals, fine non-luminous baton hands, and a clean, uncluttered layout without luminous material. Together, these details perfectly capture the understated elegance for which the Calatrava has become renowned. The watch is paired with one of our Bulang and Sons leather straps and is fitted with its original 18k yellow gold Patek Philippe pin buckle. Inside beats the ultra-thin hand-wound calibre 175, a movement celebrated for its elegant construction and reliability. It has been fully serviced by our watchmaker and is ready to be enjoyed for many years to come. There is something quietly captivating about a vintage Calatrava. Free from unnecessary distractions, it simply does everything right. This reference 3470 is no exception and is ready to be enjoyed by its next owner. description: Audemars Piguet is a Swiss watch manufacture founded in 1875 in Le Brassus by Jules Louis Audemars and Edward Auguste Piguet. It belongs to watchmaking's prestigious "Holy Trinity" and, uniquely among its peers, remains under the ownership of its founding families to this day. By the early 1970s, Audemars Piguet faced mounting pressure from the emerging Quartz Crisis. In response, Managing Director Georges Golay challenged legendary designer Gérald Genta to create an entirely new kind of watch—an elegant luxury sports watch in stainless steel. According to watchmaking lore, Genta completed the initial design overnight, drawing inspiration from a traditional diver's helmet. The result was the Royal Oak reference 5402ST. What began as a daring horological gamble would go on to redefine the luxury watch industry. Over the decades, the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak evolved from a controversial high-end sports watch into one of the world's most recognisable timepieces—a true pop culture icon embraced by Hollywood, elite athletes, musicians, and collectors alike. Offered here is a particularly rare and elegant mid-sized Royal Oak, as per information by AP; “Sales from 1978 to 1983: 131 units in all” ! Derived from the Royal Oak reference 4100, the reference 4153—renamed 14153 following Audemars Piguet's revised reference numbering system in 1984/1985—is distinguished by its bezel, which is set with 80 brilliant-cut diamonds. This style of gem-setting is characteristic of the earliest diamond-set Royal Oaks. Rather than being set into the top surface of the bezel, the diamonds were carefully positioned around its outer edge. The exceptionally thin profile of the Royal Oak bezel left insufficient material for traditional top-setting without compromising the watch's water resistance. This ingenious solution not only preserved the integrity of the case but also beautifully emphasized the Royal Oak's signature octagonal silhouette and its eight exposed white gold screws. According to Audemars Piguet's archives, only 176 examples of the reference 4153/14153 were sold between 1978 and 1985. Although these watches carry consecutive case numbers from the reference 4100 series, the manufacture's records identify them as the distinct reference 4153, making them among the rarest early gem-set Royal Oaks. title: Rolex Sea-Dweller 1665 MK3 Matte Dial
description: The Rolex Sea-Dweller was introduced in 1967 as the ultimate tool watch for professional saturation divers. Its development was driven by a very real challenge faced by the commercial deep-sea diving industry. During the 1960s, commercial divers working on pioneering saturation diving projects—such as France's COMEX and the U.S. Navy's SEALAB program—spent days living and working inside pressurised underwater habitats while breathing a helium-rich gas mixture known as Heliox. Because helium molecules are exceptionally small, they could penetrate the watch's rubber gaskets and accumulate inside the case. During decompression, the trapped helium expanded faster than it could escape, creating enough internal pressure to force the acrylic crystal from the watch. To solve this problem, Rolex co-developed and patented the Helium Escape Valve (HEV). Positioned at 9 o'clock on the case, this ingenious one-way valve automatically releases excess helium once the internal pressure reaches a critical level, preventing damage to the crystal and ensuring the watch remains watertight and fully functional. Offered here is the inaugural Sea-Dweller reference, the legendary ref. 1665, dating to 1979. The watch features a beautifully preserved case paired with a gently faded black bezel insert, giving it the unmistakable character collectors love to see. The matte black MK3 dial is in excellent condition and displays an attractive warm yellow patina across the lume plots and hands, adding just the right amount of vintage charm while remaining wonderfully balanced. The watch is fitted with an Oyster bracelet, reference 93150, complete with 585 end links and a clasp stamped "VD," all presented in excellent condition. Inside beats a movement that has been fully serviced by our watchmaker and is ready to provide many years of reliable enjoyment. The Sea-Dweller ref. 1665 is more than just another vintage Rolex—it is a genuine piece of professional diving history. Built to solve a real-world engineering challenge, it remains one of the purest expressions of Rolex's tool-watch philosophy and an essential reference for any serious vintage Rolex collection. From the depths of the ocean to the heart of a great collection, this Sea-Dweller is ready for its next custodian! title: IWC Automatic Dresswatch  Silver dial ref R810A
description: IWC Schaffhausen, or International Watch Company, was founded in 1868 by American watchmaker Florentine Ariosto Jones. His vision was an unusual one for the time: to combine American-style industrial production with the renowned craftsmanship of Swiss watchmaking. Rather than settling in the traditional watchmaking centres of the French-speaking Swiss Jura, Jones chose the German-speaking town of Schaffhausen, where the hydropower of the Rhine could help drive his ambitious new manufacture. More than 150 years later, that engineering-minded spirit is still very much part of IWC. Today part of the Richemont Group, the manufacture remains known for robust, highly legible watches and a distinctly technical approach to watchmaking. This particular Ref. R810A comes in a lovely 34mm stainless steel case, with elegant lugs and a classic press-in caseback. It is a wonderfully wearable size, giving the watch plenty of vintage presence without feeling oversized. And then there is that little detail we always enjoy finding: a Portuguese import marking on the upper left lug. For much of the 20th century, watches entering Portugal from abroad were subject to customs duties and taxation and had to pass through the Portuguese customs and assay system. The resulting punção was a small official punch applied to qualifying watches. Collectors sometimes refer to these as “Salazar marks”, although Portuguese import or Contrastaria mark is the more accurate description. The reason is beautifully simple: Switzerland and Portugal were separate customs territories, meaning that a Swiss-made IWC arriving in Portugal was a foreign import and therefore had to pass through the Portuguese system. So that tiny mark on the lug is more than just an unusual case detail — it is a little piece of the watch's journey. The silver dial is particularly charming, finished with a beautiful vertical brushing that catches the light in a wonderfully subtle way. An applied IWC logo, fine black printing and elegant hour markers keep things crisp and understated, while the date aperture sits neatly at 3 o’clock. The distinctive semi-sword hands retain their original cream-coloured tritium lume, adding just the right amount of warmth. Inside beats IWC's automatic calibre 854/8541, part of one of the manufacture's most important automatic movement families and a fine example of the robust engineering for which Schaffhausen became known. The movement has been fully serviced by our watchmaker, and the watch is fitted with a generic leather strap with an original IWC pin buckle fitted. A charming and understated vintage IWC, with a beautifully detailed dial, a wonderfully wearable 34mm case and, best of all, that little Portuguese mark quietly telling us where this particular Schaffhausen creation once travelled. title: Rolex Submariner 5512 4-liner Gilt Chapter Ring Exclamation point Dial Pointed Crown Guards Case
description: Introduced in 1959, the Rolex Submariner reference 5512 is widely regarded as one of the most important dive watches ever produced. Manufactured until approximately 1980, it established the blueprint for the modern Submariner by introducing crown guards and increasing the Oyster case to the now-classic 40mm diameter. Although it shared much of its appearance with the reference 5513, the 5512 was produced in far smaller numbers, making it one of the most sought-after vintage Submariners today. Prior to the 5512, Submariners featured "no crown guard" cases, leaving the winding crown exposed to knocks and impacts. With the 5512, Rolex introduced protective crown guards, a defining feature that would become standard across the Submariner line. Their design evolved through three distinct phases over the years. The earliest examples from 1959 featured square crown guards. While exceptionally rare today, they proved somewhat impractical, as their blocky shape made it difficult for professional divers to unscrew the crown while wearing gloves. Rolex soon replaced them with the elegant pointed crown guards—known among collectors as "PCG" or Cornino —whose tapered profile improved accessibility while giving the watch one of its most distinctive silhouettes. By 1964, the familiar rounded crown guards were introduced, a design that remained in production until the end of the reference and continues to define the Submariner to this day. The movement also evolved during production. Early reference 5512s were powered by the non-chronometer calibre 1530 and featured the clean "two-line" dial, displaying only the model designation and depth rating above six o'clock. In 1962, Rolex upgraded the 5512 with chronometer-certified calibres 1560 and later 1570. As a result, the dial gained the additional "Superlative Chronometer Officially Certified" text, creating the familiar four-line layout. That same year, Rolex introduced the reference 5513. Although nearly identical in appearance, it retained a non-chronometer movement and the simpler two-line dial, allowing Rolex to offer it at a more accessible price. The 5513 remained in production for a similar length of time and was manufactured in substantially larger numbers—estimated at nearly ten times the production of the 5512—making original 5512s considerably scarcer and especially desirable among collectors today. Offered here is an early 1963 example featuring the highly desirable pointed crown guard (PCG) case. The case remains beautifully full and strong, while the bezel insert has gracefully faded to a rich mid-blue tone. We often think of a bezel insert as the frame around a painting—the right frame makes all the difference—and this one complements the dial beautifully. The glossy gilt chapter ring dial is equally attractive and features the sought-after "Exclamation Point" configuration, named after the small lume dot positioned beneath the six o'clock marker, creating the appearance of an exclamation mark. description: Introduced in 1945 to celebrate Rolex's 40th anniversary, the Datejust changed the course of watchmaking. It became the world's first self-winding, waterproof chronometer wristwatch with an automatically changing date display—a feature we now take completely for granted. While many Rolex models were created with pilots, divers, or racing drivers in mind, the Datejust was simply designed to be the perfect everyday watch. Eight decades later, that formula still works, making it one of the most enduring and successful wristwatches ever produced. Rolex introduced reference 6605 in 1956, producing it until 1959. A true transitional model, it bridged the gap between the early Datejusts and the references that followed. It introduced the slimmer in-house calibre 1065, allowing Rolex to move away from the thicker "Bubbleback" profile while retaining the robustness for which the Oyster case had become famous. The 6605 also ranks among the earliest Datejust references to feature the now-familiar "Superlative Chronometer Officially Certified" designation on the dial, together with the Cyclops magnifying lens that had made its debut just a year earlier. Adding another charming detail is the original roulette date disc, alternating red and black numerals—a small touch that never fails to put a smile on our faces. The watch is paired with one of our own Bulang and Sons leather straps and has been fully serviced by our watchmaker, ready to be worn and enjoyed. One look at that dial, and you'll understand why we love these early Datejusts! description: Patek Philippe has a long and distinguished history with chronographs, dating back to 1856 when the manufacture produced one of its earliest chronograph pocket watches. The inspiration came after co-founder Antoine Norbert de Patek travelled to America, where he observed a growing demand for precise timing instruments—particularly for measuring the speed of horse races. In 1923, Patek Philippe created its very first chronograph wristwatch, a highly complex split-seconds timepiece capable of measuring two separate events simultaneously. By 1927, the manufacture had begun regular production of wrist chronographs, laying the foundation for what would become one of its most celebrated complications. Introduced in 1943, the reference 1579 is one of Patek Philippe's most charismatic vintage chronographs. It features an elegant 18k yellow gold three-piece case with distinctive sculptural "spider" lugs, crafted by the renowned case maker Wenger. The polished gold feuille hour and minute hands are paired with a blued central chronograph seconds hand, creating a striking contrast while maintaining outstanding legibility. During the 1940s and 1950s, before modern water-resistant case construction became commonplace, moisture and dust could occasionally affect the appearance of a dial over time. Rather than replacing these original dials, Patek Philippe trained specialist watchmakers to carefully clean and preserve and restore them whenever possible during servicing. The innovation proved so significant that Eterna adopted the five-ball bearing as its emblem—a logo that remains synonymous with the brand to this day. Some highlights from Eterna's remarkable history: 1914 – Eterna patents one of the world's first wristwatch alarm mechanisms, bringing the complication into series production. 1932 – The company is reorganized into two independent entities: Eterna, dedicated to manufacturing complete watches, and ETA SA, established to develop and supply movements—a company that would become the backbone of the Swiss watch industry. 1958 – Eterna introduces the legendary KonTiki, named in honour of Thor Heyerdahl's famous 1947 Pacific Ocean expedition aboard the Kon-Tiki raft. 1995 – The Porsche family acquires Eterna. The manufacture subsequently produces Porsche Design timepieces until 2014. Presented here is a beautiful 35mm Eterna chronograph in 18k rose gold. Developed as a professional tool for underwater exploration, it established the blueprint for the modern dive watch with its robust Oyster case, highly legible dial, rotating timing bezel, and exceptional water resistance. Over the past seven decades, it has evolved from an indispensable instrument into one of the world's most recognizable luxury sports watches. Introduced in 1969, the Rolex Submariner Date reference 1680 marked a major milestone in the model's evolution. It became the first Submariner to feature a date display and the first to incorporate Rolex's now-iconic Cyclops magnifying lens, two innovations that would go on to become defining characteristics of the Submariner collection. Presented here is a handsome 1977 example. The watch retains a lovely, full Oyster case and is fitted with a beautifully preserved fat-font bezel insert that has escaped the fading often seen on these vintage pieces. The Mk I dial is equally attractive. Collectors identify this early variation by the Rolex coronet, which aligns perfectly with the "L" in the Rolex signature. The tritium lume has aged to a rich beige tone, beautifully matched by the hands, giving the watch the warm character we all look for in a vintage Submariner. The watch is fitted with its Oyster bracelet, reference 93150, with 580 end links. Fully serviced by our watchmaker, this nearly fifty-year-old icon is ready for many more years of adventures. Half a century on, and still setting the standard. Get in touch ! The red, white, and blue sub-dial is divided into three five-minute sections, allowing sailors to time the crucial pre-start phase and gain every possible advantage. The watch also features a date display at six o'clock, funky orange accents throughout the dial, a bright orange central chronograph seconds hand, and matching orange hour and minute hands that have faded beautifully to a warm yellow hue over time.The right chrono hand has been relumed in the past. title: Rolex Air-King 5500 Black Dial Silver print
description: The Rolex Air-King reference 5500 is often considered one of the purest expressions of vintage Rolex design. Produced between 1957 and 1989, it remained remarkably consistent throughout its long production run — a simple and honest time-only watch that quietly did everything right. Free from unnecessary complications or excessive design details, the Air-King 5500 embodies Rolex’s restrained approach to watchmaking. Clean lines, balanced proportions and everyday wearability are what make these references so enduringly appealing today. One detail we particularly love on these models is the typography. The font used on many Air-King dials feels surprisingly playful and unconventional for Rolex, giving the watch a touch of charm and personality rarely seen elsewhere in the brand’s catalogue. The black dial is especially attractive, featuring unusual silver printed text and elegant marker that contrasts beautifully against the black surface and gives the watch a distinctly understated character.This fine Air-King is fully serviced by our watch maker and is fitted with a lovely Bulang and sons leather strap. title: Patek Philippe Calatrava 3919J Porcelain Dial 18k Yellow Gold Clous de Paris
description: The Patek Philippe Calatrava is widely regarded as one of the purest expressions of the classic dress watch and has become a cornerstone of 20th-century watch design. Introduced in 1932 by Patek Philippe, the Calatrava emerged during a pivotal moment in the company’s history, shortly after the Stern family acquired the manufacture amid the economic uncertainty of the Great Depression. The reference 3919 presented here was introduced during the mid-1980s, a period when the Swiss watch industry was still recovering from the effects of the Quartz Crisis. In an effort to reaffirm the timeless values of traditional watchmaking, Patek Philippe collaborated with renowned Swiss advertising strategist René Bittel to strengthen and redefine the identity of the Calatrava collection. The result was the reference 3919 — a model that elegantly combined many of the brand’s most iconic design traits into one refined and highly wearable dress watch. One of its defining characteristics is the intricate Clous de Paris guilloché bezel. Although this decorative motif first appeared on the Calatrava reference 96D in 1934, it became permanently associated with the 3919 and remains one of the most recognizable signatures of modern Calatrava design. This refined example features a crisp white porcelain dial with elegant Roman numerals, beautifully contrasted by blackened oxidized gold feuille hands and a subsidiary seconds register positioned at 6 o’clock. The proportions remain wonderfully restrained and quintessentially Patek Philippe. We have paired the watch with one of our Bulang and Sons leather straps, while the original 18k gold Patek Philippe pin buckle remains fitted. Powering the watch is the ultra-thin manually wound Calibre 215 PS (Petite Seconde), one of Patek Philippe’s most celebrated dress watch movements. The watch has been fully serviced by our watchmaker and is ready to be enjoyed for many years to come. A timeless Calatrava that perfectly captures the elegance of Patek Philippe, let’s get you this! title: Rolex Submariner 1680 Red Meters First MK2 Dial
description: The Rolex Submariner was the first wristwatch to achieve a water-resistance rating of 100 meters (330 feet). Conceived by Rolex director and passionate diver René-Paul Jeanneret, it was developed as a specialised tool for both professional and recreational diving, while remaining elegant and practical enough for everyday wear. Introduced at Baselworld in 1954, the Submariner would go on to become one of the most influential sports watches ever produced. In 1969, Rolex introduced the Submariner Date with the launch of reference 1680. For the first time, the Submariner featured a date display at 3 o’clock together with Rolex’s now-iconic Cyclops magnification lens, designed to improve legibility underwater and in daily use alike. Early examples of the 1680 are especially prized for one small but highly important detail: the word “Submariner” printed in red. This subtle variation would later earn the nickname “Red Sub” and has since become one of the most celebrated and collectible configurations in the world of vintage Rolex collecting. Presented here is exactly that — an early Submariner reference 1680 “Red Sub” preserved in excellent overall condition. The watch retains a strong and beautifully proportioned case and is fitted with an equally attractive fat-font bezel insert that has faded over time to a rich dark blue hue, adding tremendous character to the watch. The dial is a highly collectible “Meters First” Mark II variant, referring to the depth rating being displayed in metric before imperial measurements (“200m = 660ft”). These early dials are particularly sought after, representing a brief transitional period before Rolex switched to “Feet First” printing to better suit the rapidly growing American market, which had become the brand’s largest consumer base at the time. This fine Submariner is fitted with a Rolex folded Oyster bracelet, reference 9315, complete with end links stamped 280 and a clasp dated 1/71 — a wonderfully period-correct combination that perfectly complements the watch’s overall character. The watch and its movement have been fully serviced and are running like an absolute dream. An iconic reference that perfectly captures the spirit of vintage Rolex sports watches! title: Rolex Cosmograph Daytona 16523 Black Inverted 6 Dial Executed in Steel and 18k Yellow Gold
description: Introduced in 1963, the Rolex Cosmograph Daytona was designed as a purpose-built chronograph for professional racing drivers, featuring its distinctive tachymeter bezel for measuring average speeds. Although initially a slow seller, it has since evolved into one of the most iconic and collectible wristwatches ever produced. For the first 25 years of its existence, every Daytona was manually wound. Recognising the need for a more modern chronograph, Rolex introduced the Reference 16520 in 1988—the brand's first self-winding Daytona. As Rolex had not yet developed its own automatic chronograph movement, it extensively reworked Zenith's legendary El Primero calibre, replacing roughly half of its components to meet Rolex's exacting standards. At the same time, the case diameter grew from 37 mm to 40 mm, the acrylic crystal made way for sapphire, and the dial received a more contemporary design with glossy lacquer and applied metal surrounds to the subdials. Presented here is the Reference 16523, the handsome Rolesor version combining stainless steel with 18 ct yellow gold. This particular example remains in excellent condition, with a strong case retaining thick lugs, well-defined crown guards, and a beautifully preserved "Units per Hour" bezel. The glossy black dial features the sought-after "inverted 6", where the numeral in the lower chronograph register is printed upside down—a small but desirable detail appreciated by Daytona collectors. The boat-shaped hour markers and matching hands have developed a warm beige patina, perfectly complementing the deep black dial and champagne-coloured subdials. The watch is fitted with its steel and yellow gold Oyster bracelet, reference 78363, complete with reference 403 end links and an M8-stamped clasp. The watch and its automatic movement have been fully serviced by our watchmaker and are ready to be enjoyed for many years to come. Early Zenith-powered Daytonas continue to attract a growing following among collectors, and the two-tone Reference 16523 remains one of the most wearable and characterful variants. For further information or to arrange a private viewing, please get in touch. title: Rolex GMT-Master II 16710 Tritium Dial
description: The Rolex GMT-Master is one of the most iconic travel watches ever created. Introduced in 1955, it was developed in collaboration with Pan American Airways (Pan Am) to meet the needs of long-haul airline pilots who required a simple way to track multiple time zones during international flights. A major milestone came in 1982 with the introduction of the GMT-Master II, reference 16760. This new generation featured an independently adjustable hour hand, allowing the wearer to track multiple time zones more conveniently than ever before. The GMT-Master II would eventually replace the original GMT-Master and become one of Rolex's flagship professional models. The reference 16710 offered here, introduced in 1989, is widely considered one of the most versatile and beloved GMT-Master II references. Produced for nearly twenty years, it was available with several bezel inserts, including the iconic Pepsi (red and blue), Coke (red and black), and all-black versions. Combining a slim case profile, aluminium bezel insert, and the robust calibre 3185 movement, the 16710 represents the perfect balance between vintage charm and modern practicality. The case of this fine GMT-Master II remains in great condition and is fitted with a lovely black bezel insert showing only minimal signs of wear. The dial is signed "Swiss T-25" at six o'clock, denoting the use of tritium, and remains in outstanding condition. The Oyster bracelet, reference 78790, is equally well preserved and fitted with 501B end links and a clasp stamped X4. The watch has been fully checked and regulated by our watchmaker and is ready for many years of reliable service. The ultimate travel watch, just in time for summer adventures. If this GMT-Master II belongs on your wrist, we'd love to hear from you ! Despite being more than a century old, its design remains strikingly modern and relevant today. While traditional Tank models are known for their sharp, straight lines, the Tank Arrondie—French for "rounded"—offers a softer interpretation of the classic design. Conceived in 1976 and officially launched in 1977, the Arrondie features elegantly curved brancards that create a smooth, cushion-like profile, making it exceptionally comfortable on the wrist. Further details include the classic railroad minute track, Cartier's discreet hidden signature within the VII numeral, and the Tank's signature black Roman numerals, all combining to create a dial that is both elegant and unmistakably Cartier. The hand-wound movement is based on the ultra-thin mechanical Calibre 21, created by the renowned Swiss watchmaker Frédéric Piguet. title: Vacheron Constantin Coin Watch in 18k Yellow Gold 4928
description: Founded in 1755, Vacheron Constantin is the oldest watch manufacturer in the world to have operated continuously without interruption. Based in Geneva, Switzerland, the Maison has spent more than 270 years crafting exceptional timepieces that blend technical mastery with refined artistic expression. Widely regarded as part of the prestigious “Holy Trinity” of Swiss watchmaking, alongside Patek Philippe and Audemars Piguet, the brand has long stood at the pinnacle of haute horlogerie. Throughout its history, Vacheron Constantin has served royalty, collectors, and connoisseurs alike, earning a reputation for uncompromising craftsmanship, elegant design, and mechanical innovation. Every creation reflects centuries of accumulated expertise, making the manufacture one of the most respected names in Swiss watchmaking. Coin watches are among the most extra ordinary and collectible expressions of horology. These rare creations sit at the intersection of watchmaking, numismatics, and history. Each piece begins as a genuine coin in circulation before being meticulously transformed by a master craftsman. The coin is carefully hollowed out on both sides, a concealed cavity is created to house a miniature movement, and the two halves are then reassembled with a discreet hinged opening system. Among the maisons known for producing such remarkable timepieces is Vacheron Constantin. This exceptional example is crafted from a 1904 twenty-dollar gold coin and is identified by the manufacture as Model 4928. It represents a striking combination of historical significance, technical ingenuity, and refined watchmaking, resulting in a highly collectible and visually captivating work of art. The coin opens via a side-mounted push button, revealing the hidden watch within. Inside, a small champagne-toned dial features painted hour markers and elegant blued stick hands, complemented by a discreet crown positioned at 1 o’clock. The case can also be displayed upright, transforming the piece into a functional desk or table clock—an object designed to be both worn and admired. This example is based on a 1904 twenty-dollar U.S. gold coin with a finely detailed reeded edge and straight lugs. It is fitted with its original Vacheron Constantin strap and a period-correct 18k gold “AW” signed buckle. A Bulang and Sons strap will be supplied with the watch, with the final choice left to the buyer. The hand-wound movement has been fully serviced by our watchmaker and is ready for years of reliable use. We love these Coin watches —they are effortlessly cool, lightweight on the wrist, and an absolute conversation starter! Take a closer look, and let’s have a conversation about this remarkable piece ! title: Rolex Oyster-Precision Flat Back ref. 2765 Creme Brûlée Dial
description: The Rolex reference 2765, often referred to by collectors as the “Flatback,” can best be described as the manual-winding counterpart to the famous Bubble Back models, such as the reference 2764. Produced during the early years of the Oyster era, it represents an important chapter in Rolex's pursuit of durable and waterproof wristwatches. Sharing the same elegant case profile and dimensions as its Bubble Back sibling, the reference 2765 offers all the charm of these pioneering Oyster models while delivering a distinctly different wearing experience. Unlike the Bubble Back, which housed a thicker automatic movement and required a more pronounced case back, the Flatback is powered by a slimmer manual-winding movement. As a result, it sits noticeably closer to the wrist, offering a refined and comfortable fit. Today, the reference 2765 is appreciated not only for its historical significance as one of Rolex's earliest waterproof watches, but also for its balanced proportions, understated elegance, and rarity among early Oyster references. The case is presented in excellent condition and features characteristic hooded lugs, single-sided lug holes, and a smooth bezel. Clean and well preserved throughout, it retains its Oyster “Patent” crown, an attractive detail that further reinforces its early Oyster heritage. The dial has developed a wonderfully charming patina over the decades. Its creamy surface almost reminds us of a perfectly made creme brûlée dessert—a look that can only be created by time itself. A fine minute track frames the dial, while the small seconds register at 6 o’clock provides pleasing symmetry. The even numerals are displayed in elegant Arabic form, while the odd hours are marked by delicate baton indexes, all executed in a warm copper tone. Completing the composition are a pair of fine blued hands that add a beautiful touch of contrast and sophistication. Elegant, honest, and full of character, this Flatback perfectly illustrates why these early Oyster references continue to captivate vintage Rolex collectors nearly a century after they were made.The watch and its handwound movement has been fully serviced by our watch maker. A wonderfully preserved early Oyster offering a rare glimpse into the foundations of Rolex's legendary history, this Flatback is a subtle masterpiece for collectors seeking something beyond the usual suspects! title: Tudor Submariner 7928 MK7 Dial Black-Out Lume
description: The Tudor Submariner is widely regarded as one of the most important and enduring dive watches in horological history, remaining in production from 1954 until its discontinuation in 1999. Created under the vision of Hans Wilsdorf, Tudor was established to deliver the same reliability, robustness, and waterproof performance associated with Rolex, but at a more accessible price point. The Submariner perfectly embodied this philosophy, combining true tool-watch functionality with timeless design and military-grade dependability. At hand we have a late-series reference 7928, presented in very nice overall condition, featuring a strong case and a beautifully faded “fat font” bezel insert. The Tudor Submariner 7928 is closely associated with military use, most notably by U.S. Navy SEALs and Underwater Demolition Teams (UDT) during the Vietnam War era. Documented examples are often linked to so-called “Coronado dials,” with custom modifications carried out in the field or by military watchmakers in Coronado, California, to reduce reflectivity and improve legibility during covert operations. These modifications could include reprinted or hand-painted dials, matte black finishes, and the removal or darkening of luminous material on the indexes and hands. The dial on this example exhibits a similar character, with a darkened, on the original tritium lume appearance on both the markers and hands. It gives the watch a distinctive “dark horse” presence on the wrist—subtle, utilitarian, and full of character. Further enhancing its appeal, the watch features the iconic Tudor rose logo on the Mk7 dial variant. It is fitted to a “Hecho en México” Jubilee bracelet—originally produced for the North and South American markets—which adds an additional layer of period-correct charm and intrigue to this already highly collectible Tudor Submariner. We love finding watches with character, and this one certainly delivers. Get in touch if you'd like to add it to your collection. title: Heuer Autavia Black Dial ref 7763C Compressor Case
description: The story of the Heuer Autavia is one of evolution—from dashboard instruments to the wrist—spanning decades of motorsport and aviation heritage. Its name itself, a contraction of AUTomobile and AVIAtion, already hints at its purpose. First introduced in 1933 as a dashboard timer, the Autavia was designed for both sectors. It wasn’t until 1962 that Jack Heuer reimagined it as a wristwatch chronograph—marking the beginning of one of Heuer’s most iconic lines. From there, it quickly became associated with the golden era of Formula 1, worn by drivers such as Jo Siffert, Mario Andretti, and Gilles Villeneuve. The example offered here is a late 1960s reference 7763C, housed in a 40 mm case produced by Ervin Piquerez S.A.—better known for its “compressor” cases. This clever construction was designed to improve water resistance, using increasing external pressure to further compress the case gaskets. In other words, the deeper you went, the tighter it sealed—a beautiful piece of engineering from the era. The case remains in great condition and is fitted with a finely toothed rotating bezel, which has developed a subtle fade towards a soft blue hue—adding just the right amount of character. Its reverse panda dial offers a wonderful contrast, with two sub-dials set against a black background. The crisp white chronograph seconds hand adds a touch of sportiness, while the lume has aged to a warm yellow tone, giving the watch a balanced and harmonious appearance.The watch is fitted by one of our Bulang and sons leather straps of which we think as a nice match . Powered by the reliable hand-wound Valjoux 7730 movement, this chronograph has been fully serviced by our watchmaker and is ready to be worn and enjoyed. A piece that captures the spirit of an era—where function, design, and motorsport heritage came together in the most effortless way ! title: IWC/Porsche design compass watch in titanium ref 3511 with Certificate of Authenticity  paper and IWC service invoice
description: In 1977–78, Porsche Design (founded by Ferdinand “Butzi” Porsche) approached IWC with the idea of creating a wristwatch with a built-in compass. Butzi wanted something functional, bold, and distinctly different. It was a challenging time for Swiss watchmakers — the quartz crisis was sharply reducing demand for mechanical watches. IWC saw this collaboration as an opportunity to innovate and tap into new markets. The first model in the series, Ref. 3510, was launched in the late 1970s. It featured an aluminum case with a PVD or anodized coating, available in black or NATO olive green. Fast forward to 1991: the newly designed Ref. 3511 was introduced. It featured a titanium case with a ribbed or "coin-edge" finish and a repositioned crown at 4 o’clock. The dial was classic Porsche Design — minimalist and functional — with a thin crosshair layout, yellow tritium lume, white hour and minute hands, and a dark orange seconds hand. On the lower (6 o’clock) side of the case, two discreet push-buttons open the watch face to reveal the integrated compass. This example comes fitted on its original IWC flat-link titanium bracelet and fits wrists up to 20 cm. Included in the sale is a certificate of authenticity dated 1993, an IWC service invoice from 2016, and an original IWC booklet. This unique tool watch has been fully checked and regulated by our watchmaker — its Caliber 375.23 is running smoothly. This cool neo-vintage piece offers excellent value in today’s market. title: Rolex Day-Date 1803 Khanjar Sigma Champagne Dial
description: The Rolex Day-Date, introduced in 1956, marked a significant milestone in watchmaking as the world’s first wristwatch to display both the date and the day of the week fully spelled out on the dial. Positioned at the very top of the Rolex catalogue, the Day-Date has exclusively been produced in precious metals — including 18k yellow, white, or rose gold, as well as platinum — reinforcing its status as the brand’s ultimate flagship model! The present watch is a classic 36 mm 18k yellow gold reference 1803, featuring a beautifully preserved case and crisp fluted bezel. While the watch itself is undeniably elegant, the true highlight of this example is undoubtedly its dial!! It features what is arguably the quintessential Day-Date configuration: a sunburst champagne dial with contrasting black printed text, enhanced by a Sigma designation at six o’clock — denoting that the hands and hour markers are crafted from gold. Most notably, the dial proudly bears a rare red Omani Khanjar emblem, adding a fascinating layer of historical significance and collectability. For those less familiar with the emblem, the Omani Khanjar is a traditional ceremonial dagger and one of the most important national symbols of Oman, representing pride, heritage, and status. From the 1970s onward, Qaboos bin Said al Said became widely known for commissioning specially ordered watches adorned with the royal Khanjar crest, either printed on the dial or engraved on the case back. These pieces were typically gifted to high-ranking military officers, diplomats, loyal advisers, and prominent figures within the Sultan’s inner circle, giving them both exceptional rarity and strong historical importance. Many of these special commissions were supplied through Asprey of New Bond Street in London, the Sultan’s official jeweller during the era. Today, Asprey-delivered Khanjar-signed Rolex watches are regarded among the most collectible and desirable special-order vintage Rolex models ever produced, with well-preserved examples becoming increasingly difficult to source. As the flagship model of the Genevan manufacturer, it has long been synonymous with success, frequently seen on the wrists of heads of state, royalty, and other influential figures. Most Day-Dates were fitted with discreet, conservative dials—after all, most buyers of this model preferred elegance over extravagance. But Rolex made a notable exception to this unwritten rule: beginning in the 1970s, they introduced bright, high-gloss lacquered dials known today as “Stella” dials. At the time, these bold colours were not widely embraced, precisely because they attracted attention. As a result, production numbers remained low, making them highly sought after today. A wide array of colours is known—yellow, green, orange, red ,pink and multiple shades of blue, some embellished with gemstones, and produced across different metals. They also span various generations: from the early 18xx “pie-pan” versions to the later 18xxx models with flat dials. The manufacturing process was exceptionally labor-intensive. Each dial was spray-painted and then oven-baked to set the pigment. This cycle was repeated multiple times until the desired depth of colour and finish was achieved. Afterward, the dial was polished and coated with a clear lacquer. This final step created the distinctive effect where the printed text appears to float above the glossy surface, reminiscent of the porcelain-dial Daytonas. description: The name Calatrava traces its origins to medieval Spain, referring both to a fortress in the Castile region and to a chivalric order founded in 1157, established to defend it. The Order of Calatrava adopted a distinctive emblem—a red Greek cross with fleur-de-lis tips—a symbol that would later take on an entirely new significance in the world of watchmaking. In 1887, Patek Philippe selected this cross as part of its official trademark, registering it alongside the name Patek Philippe & Cie . The exact reasoning behind this choice has never been clearly documented. It may simply have been the strength and elegance of the design, or perhaps a deeper symbolic link to values such as tradition, discipline, and longevity. Whatever the case, the Calatrava cross appeared only sparingly on the brand’s early watches. Notably, Calatrava was not initially used as a model designation. It was only in the 1980s that the name formally entered Patek Philippe’s catalogue. Nevertheless, collectors and historians retrospectively adopted the term to describe the brand’s refined, time-only dress watches of the 1930s—most famously beginning with Reference 96—thereby establishing the Calatrava as a cornerstone of Patek Philippe’s design language. Since the introduction of the Calatrava in 1932, Patek Philippe has produced well over 100 distinct references. The collection has evolved continuously, encompassing a wide range of executions, from classic time-only models and officer-style cases to more recent and complex interpretations such as Annual Calendar and Pilot Travel Time models. Offered here is a beautiful time-only Calatrava, reference 3513, crafted in 18k white gold. It features a clean, flat bezel, a snap-back 31 mm case, and a small winding crown set with a black-topped cabochon. The watch is fitted with a finely crafted integrated 18k white gold bracelet, finished by hand with a striking hammered effect—a detail that speaks volumes about the level of craftsmanship involved. The bracelet comfortably fits wrists up to approximately 18–18.5 cm and is secured by an elegant clasp adorned with the iconic Calatrava cross. The dial is finished in a soft silver tone, complemented by black painted Roman numerals and simple black stick hands, with no luminous material—pure, understated elegance. At its heart is the hand-wound calibre 175, fully serviced by our watchmaker and running beautifully. An elegant and increasingly elusive white-gold Calatrava, this reference perfectly embodies Patek Philippe's enduring philosophy of understated luxury and timeless design. An elegant addition to any serious collection! title: Rolex Day-Date 18078 Green Khanjar Champagne Dial Bark Finish in 18k Yellow Gold
description: The Rolex Day-Date, introduced in 1956, marked a significant milestone in watchmaking as the world’s first wristwatch to display both the date and the day of the week fully spelled out on the dial. Positioned at the very top of the Rolex catalogue, the Day-Date has exclusively been produced in precious metals — including 18k yellow, white, or Everose gold, as well as platinum — reinforcing its status as the brand’s ultimate flagship model. The model became closely associated with the iconic “President” bracelet, a semi-circular three-link design created specifically for the Day-Date’s launch. While the bracelet itself carried the “President” name, the nickname soon became synonymous with the entire watch. The Day-Date’s association with influential world leaders further elevated its legendary status. Dwight D. Eisenhower famously received a Rolex from the brand, while Lyndon B. Johnson was often seen wearing a yellow gold Day-Date during his presidency. Over the decades, the model has become an enduring symbol of prestige, success, and leadership, worn by presidents, executives, and cultural icons around the world. This particular example features several highly desirable and seldom-seen characteristics. It is preserved in the rare reference 18078 configuration, distinguished by its hand-finished “bark” decoration — a textured motif applied to both the bezel and President bracelet, designed to resemble the natural grain of tree bark. This intricate finish gives the watch a striking and unmistakably luxurious appearance. The champagne dial is beautifully balanced and elevated further by an exceptionally rare green Omani Khanjar and crown signature printed on the left side of the dial. Additional details include a finely printed railroad minute track, warm cream-coloured lume plots, and an English day disc. For those unfamiliar with the symbol, the Omani Khanjar is a traditional curved dagger worn ceremonially in Oman, representing heritage, honour, and national pride. During the 1970s onward, Qaboos bin Said al Said became renowned for commissioning specially ordered watches featuring the royal Khanjar crest, either printed on the dial or engraved on the case back. These watches were typically presented to senior military officials, diplomats, trusted advisers, and members of the Sultan’s inner circle, making them objects of both extraordinary rarity and important historical significance. Many of these bespoke commissions were supplied through Asprey of New Bond Street, London, the Sultan’s preferred jeweller during the period. Watches retailed through Asprey — particularly Rolex models bearing the Khanjar emblem — have since become some of the most coveted and elusive special-order timepieces in the world of vintage Rolex collecting. These oversized cases were mostly used from the 1940s until around 1960 by brands like Vacheron Constantin, Omega, Longines, and others. Universal Genève (UG) was founded in 1894 as Universal Watch in Le Locle, Switzerland, by Numa Descombes and Ulysse Perret. The brand specialized in both watch movements and cases. After relocating to Geneva in 1919, UG gained prominence for its high-quality chronographs. and time only pieces like the iconic Compax and Polerouter models—and for its innovative micro-rotor automatic movements. The brand’s fortunes declined after the quartz crisis of the 1970s, but in 2023, the name was acquired by Breitling, signaling a potential revival and return to its legacy of excellence. title: Rolex Submariner 5513 MilSub with Rolex Service Card
description: Say “MilSub” to a watch collector and you might just see them go weak at the knees—or momentarily lost for words. The Rolex Military Submariner, or “MilSub,” was produced in the 1970s in extremely small quantities (just over 1,000 pieces), of which only a few hundred are believed to survive today. It’s no surprise these watches are considered true grails—often commanding between €200k and €500k depending on condition and provenance. But what’s the story behind these rare Submariners? Although produced in the 1970s, the MilSub’s origins trace back to World War II and the rise of underwater combat operations. The Italians were early pioneers in this field, using Panerai watches—interestingly manufactured by Rolex at the time. Great Britain soon followed, commissioning purpose-built watches capable of withstanding prolonged underwater missions. After the war, this evolved into ongoing diving operations within the British Ministry of Defence (MoD), which required reliable, purpose-built wristwatches. By 1957, the MoD approached Rolex with a clear set of specifications. Rolex responded by adapting its Submariner with fixed spring bars, a larger bezel for operation with gloves, and dials using tritium lume (marked by the encircled “T”) instead of the more hazardous radium. For a brief period, the MoD turned to Omega, commissioning military versions of the Seamaster 300. However, in the early 1970s, they returned to Rolex—likely due to the superior water resistance offered by Rolex’s screw-down crown system. One requirement carried over from the Omega designs was the use of “sword hands,” providing greater lume surface and improved underwater legibility. The Submariner reference 5513 was subsequently modified to meet these specifications. Changes included fixed bars, a fully graduated 60-minute bezel insert, a matte dial, and the distinctive sword hands. Over the course of the 1970s, these watches underwent subtle evolutions. Early examples were marked “5513” between the lugs, followed by versions bearing both “5513” and “5517,” with the final series marked solely “5517.” These watches were issued primarily to two branches of the British military: Army (W10 designation) Case backs were engraved with: W10 (MoD code for the Army) 6645 (NATO code for time-measuring instruments) 99 (NATO country code for the UK) 923-7697 (NATO code for divers’ watches) Broad Arrow marking Issue number and year Royal Navy (0552 designation) Case backs were engraved with: 0552 (Royal Navy service code) 923-7697 (NATO code for divers’ watches) Broad Arrow marking Issue number and year Inside the case back of a correct MilSub, one would typically find engravings indicating the model reference, the date of manufacture for the case or case back, and—depending on the batch—the serial number matching the case. title: Rolex Chronograph ref. 4500 Pulsations Dial
description: The Rolex Chronograph ref. 4500, introduced around 1945, is a historically significant and rare example of one of the earliest waterproof Oyster chronographs, often referred to as the “Monoblocco” due to its one-piece case design. It marked a key design shift toward the later “modern” Daytona, with a 36mm size, straight lugs, and a two-register layout powered by a Valjoux 23–based movement. The case on this example is in excellent condition, featuring a screw-down back, pump-style pushers, and its original winding crown still attached. The true showstopper is the extremely rare pulsations dial. The pulso meter scale was primarily designed for medical professionals, namely doctors. pulsations -signed Rolex chronographs are extraordinarily rare, with approximately 50 pieces known across all metals and references. The lineage of these “medical” chronographs includes very early references such as 2023 and 2057 from the late 1920s, the “Bariletto” reference 3525 in steel during the 1940s, as well as references 4048, 4062, 4099, 4537 (in stainless steel or stainless steel and gold), and the ref. 4500 in gold. In the 1950s, the pulso meter scale appeared on some examples of the 6034 and 6234 in stainless steel and gold, followed by a handful of ref. 6238s with the scale inside the indexes, and finally around ten examples of the ref. 6239 Daytona in steel. After this period, Rolex ceased producing pulsometer dials for over 60 years, and they remain absent in modern production. This particular dial features a French-language pulso meter scale in blue (‘Gradué pour 30 pulsations’), suggesting it was likely made on special request for a French-speaking doctor. Such dials were extremely rare and difficult to produce in batches due to very low demand. The dial also features a fine black seconds track, two sub dials, applied Arabic numerals, and arrowhead hour markers, all showing pleasing patina. It is topped with clean non-lumed stick-style hands, completing a truly remarkable vintage chronograph. The watch is paired with an Oyster riveted-style ref 7206 bracelet, with end links marked 60 and a clasp stamped 1/60. This fine doctor’s chronograph and its hand-wound Cal. VLJX.23 movement have been fully serviced by our watchmaker. One of approximately 50 known pulsations examples across all references and a true collector’s find—reach out to secure this rare doctor’s Rolex chronograph! With the 5960, Patek Philippe advanced this complication by incorporating a chronograph module, providing a modern alternative to their traditional perpetual chronographs like the 5970/5270. This marked the debut of an in-house chronograph movement and set the stage alongside the Nautilus chronograph 5980, establishing a new classic. Since its launch, various iterations of the 5960 have emerged, but we are excited to present an example in its original configuration: the platinum case model featuring a striking grey soleil dial. The watch remains in excellent condition, having been preserved in great condition and seen minimal wrist time. We see this watch as an undervalued gem, overlooked yet poised to become a future classic due to its outstanding design and historical significance. The company, now known as IWC Schaffhausen, is a renowned watch manufacturer that has expanded into wristwatches and innovative materials while remaining true to its engineering-focused philosophy. The IWC Portofino collection evolved from a design inspired by a classic pocket watch and has since become one of IWC's most successful lines, known for its understated elegance and timeless aesthetics. The full Portofino collection was officially launched in 1984, named after the picturesque Italian fishing village to evoke the spirit of la dolce vita . Worn by men as a symbol of status, masculinity, and national pride, it forms part of the traditional Omani dress for formal, religious, and celebratory occasions. Often ornately decorated, the khanjar is also the national emblem of Oman. This watch was gifted to someone special by the late Sultan Qaboos bin Said al Said. In the watch-collecting world, it is well known that the Sultan was an avid admirer of fine timepieces, and quite a number of Rolex, Cartier, and IWC models bearing this emblem are documented. This Portofino comes on its original IWC leather strap, fitted with a steel IWC pin buckle. description: The 1950s proved to be a defining era for Rolex, highlighted by the introduction of some of its most legendary models: the Submariner, GMT-Master, Day-Date, and Explorer lines. As scuba diving gained traction among adventurers and professionals alike, Rolex recognized the growing demand for a dependable dive watch to help monitor time spent underwater and reduce the risk of decompression sickness, also known as “the bends.” There was also a need for a reliable timing device to track the remaining “breathing time.” This vision culminated in the creation of the Submariner—a timepiece that would come to represent not only technical excellence and rugged reliability but also timeless design. The Rolex Submariner reference 6205 was introduced in 1954 as one of the earliest Submariner models, alongside references 6204 and 6200. The 6205 was produced for only about a year, making it a rare and highly sought-after collector's item. As Rolex themselves put it in the book Oyster Perpetual Submariner: The Watch That Unlocked the Deep , just 810 examples were produced. To put that in perspective: approximately 2,800 reference 6538 "Big Crown" Submariners were made. A signficant innovation of the 6205 was the introduction of the "Submariner" name on the dial, a feature that has remained on all subsequent Submariner models, so maybe we can conclude this is the “real “first Submariner! The “ no depth rating “ dial is still in nice condition, with the original pencil and “lollipop” seconds hands present. Although the hands have been re-lumed in the pas they still look charming. The 37.5 mm “small crown “ case stays in nice condition .The so-called “no-hash” bezel insert remains on the watch in unmolested condition, though we believe the bezel itself is a later replacement and has been paired with one of our leather straps. This super early “Neanderthaler” Sub has been fully serviced by our watchmaker and is ready to join a Submariner-themed collection. We've enjoyed this watch for some time, and it has truly grown on us. Get in touch. title: Blancpain Fifty Fathoms "No Rad" Date
description: The Fifty Fathoms was originally developed in collaboration with the French Navy’s elite combat divers—and its legacy lives on today, even in modern pop culture, thanks to the recent Blancpain × Swatch Bioceramic Scuba collection. But if you’ve got the Swatch, you really need to experience the original. This is a desirable 41mm example in beautiful, honest condition—exactly what we love to see. The name Fifty Fathoms might sound unusual, but it refers to a British unit of measurement. A fathom equals about six feet, so fifty fathoms translates to roughly 91 meters—close to 300 feet—the maximum depth divers could reach with the technology available at the time. Fifty Fathoms watches have seen serious military use over the decades, trusted by forces from France, Germany, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Finland, and most famously, the U.S. Navy. This particular version is the highly sought-after "No Radiations" model, often nicknamed the “No-Rad.” What makes it special? That iconic yellow-and-red crossed-out radiation symbol on the dial. It signified that no radium was used in the luminous material—a move made in the early 1960s as the health risks of radium became more widely known. The “No Rad” logo offered peace of mind to both professional and recreational divers. Due to their historical significance—and that instantly recognizable symbol—these models are now highly prized by collectors. Blancpain has even released tribute editions of the Fifty Fathoms No Rad, cementing its place in the brand’s history. The matte case is in fine condition with a beautiful luminous rotating dive bezel. Schild caliber AS.1700) has been fully serviced by our watchmaker. For collectors and enthusiasts, the "No Rad" is more than just a beautiful timepiece—it’s a symbol of a bygone era when watches were true tools built for survival. Let’s talk. title: Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Ref. 6001ST
description: The reference 6001 is a watch you’re unlikely to have encountered before. It’s not a Royal Oak, designed by Jean-Fred Meylan (not Gérald Genta), and visually, it shares little in common with any other Audemars Piguet model, aside from its small tapisserie dial. Fewer than 350 pieces are believed to have been produced between 1974 and 1978, after which it was replaced by the reference 6005, which bears a much closer resemblance to the Royal Oak (though it’s not called that!). The 6001 was a bold experiment, introduced during the height of the "quartz revolution." In the end, Audemars Piguet embraced quartz technology, using a modified Beta 21 movement from Omega, known as the 'megaquartz' for its remarkable 2,359,296 vibrations per second. This movement would lose or gain no more than one second per month. That small pusher near the crown? It’s used to fine-tune the time by correcting that single second. The "rounded yet octagonal" case has soft, flowing edges, far removed from the angular lines of the original Royal Oak. It has a very 1970s, almost Star Wars-esque vibe mixed with Royal Oak influences—a design that feels both futuristic and retro at the same time! The 35 x 40 mm steel case remains in excellent condition, and the integrated AP bracelet (which fits wrists up to 18 cm) is also in great shape. The signature petite tapisserie dial is in blue, featuring an applied AP logo on the lower half (just as the original Royal Oak 5402 would have had during its era!) with a date at 6 o’clock. The hands are typical of AP’s design, with the first series of Royal Oak tritium markers. The quartz-driven movement (caliber 2510) has been fully checked by our watchmaker and a fresh battery is fitted. This is a rare watch from one of the “Holy Trinity” of watch brands. Come on, guys—this is a conversation piece and super cool! Get in touch!
